# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone of therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in patients at risk for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. Although transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) have demonstrated robust efficacy in landmark trials [2,3], their reliance on intravascular and intracardiac leads carries well-recognized risks, including lead failure, venous occlusion, and systemic infection requiring complex extraction [4,5]. The entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to circumvent these lead-related complications by avoiding the vasculature and heart altogether [6].

## Device Design and Rationale

The S-ICD comprises a pulse generator implanted in a lateral thoracic pocket and a single subcutaneous lead positioned parasternally [6]. Sensing occurs through three vectors between the lead electrodes and the can, and the system delivers an 80-joule shock—substantially higher than transvenous devices because energy must traverse the chest wall [7]. The conceptual foundation was established in early work demonstrating that a totally subcutaneous configuration could reliably defibrillate [6]. Because the S-ICD provides no long-term bradycardia pacing and cannot deliver antitachycardia pacing (ATP), appropriate patient selection is essential [8].

## Clinical Evidence

The pivotal IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry provided the initial demonstration of safety and efficacy, reporting high rates of successful conversion of induced ventricular fibrillation and acceptable complication profiles [7,9]. Pooled analyses of these cohorts confirmed durable performance over extended follow-up [10]. The combined EFFORTLESS-IDE dataset showed effective termination of spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias and a low rate of device-related infection requiring extraction [11].

The landmark PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized comparison of the S-ICD with the TV-ICD in patients without a pacing indication [12]. It demonstrated noninferiority of the S-ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks, with fewer lead-related complications offset by a numerically higher rate of inappropriate shocks early in the trial [12]. The UNTOUCHED study subsequently reported low inappropriate shock rates in a primary-prevention population with reduced ejection fraction, attributable largely to refined screening, conditional shock zone programming, and the SMART Pass filter [13,14].

## Patient Selection and Screening

Mandatory preimplant electrocardiographic screening assesses adequacy of the sensing vectors to minimize T-wave oversensing, a principal cause of inappropriate shocks [15]. Screening can be performed manually using a template tool or via automated algorithms, and exercise or postural screening may identify dynamic sensing failures [16]. The S-ICD is particularly attractive for younger patients, those with channelopathies and cardiomyopathies such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, patients on hemodialysis, and individuals with limited or compromised venous access [17,18]. Conversely, patients requiring bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or ATP for recurrent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia are generally not candidates [8,19].

## Complications and Limitations

Inappropriate shocks—driven by cardiac oversensing (T-wave, R-wave double counting) and extracardiac noise such as myopotentials—remain the predominant concern, although programming refinements and dual-zone configurations have markedly reduced their incidence [14,20]. Infection rates are comparable to or lower than transvenous systems, and when infection occurs, device removal is simpler given the absence of intravascular hardware [21]. Other reported complications include pocket hematoma, lead migration, and erosion [9,22]. The inability to provide pacing therapy means that bradycardia and the need for ATP after implantation may necessitate system revision [19]. Defibrillation testing at implantation, traditionally recommended, has been re-examined, with data suggesting selective testing may be reasonable [23].

## Implantation Technique and Innovations

Refinements in implantation, notably the two-incision intermuscular technique, have improved cosmetic outcomes and reduced complications compared with the original three-incision approach [24,25]. Optimal generator and lead positioning, confirmed by the PRAETORIAN score derived from chest radiography, predicts defibrillation success and may obviate routine intraoperative testing [26].

## Future Directions

A major limitation—the lack of pacing—is being addressed through the integration of the S-ICD with leadless pacemakers, enabling communicating modular systems that can provide ATP and bradycardia pacing without transvenous leads [27,28]. Early feasibility studies of such modular cardiac rhythm management platforms are encouraging [28]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest the S-ICD is economically reasonable in appropriately selected populations, particularly those at higher risk of lead complications [29]. Ongoing comparative effectiveness research and longer-term registry data will further clarify the optimal role of the S-ICD within the broader landscape of SCD prevention [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD represents a meaningful advance in defibrillation therapy, offering protection from SCD while eliminating the risks inherent to transvenous leads. Robust randomized and registry evidence supports its safety and efficacy in appropriately selected patients without pacing needs [12,13]. As modular leadless pacing technologies mature, the principal limitation of the S-ICD may be overcome, broadening its applicability in the coming years [27,28].
